24:
Cost Explorer is the cost-analysis tool with granular filtering and grouping (by instance type, tag, account, usage) and keeps 12 months of history. Comparing the last 2 months of EC2 spend broken down by instance type is a few clicks, with nothing to build.

Why not the others: AWS Budgets sets thresholds and alerts on forecasted spend, not deep historical analysis. The Billing and Cost Management dashboard shows high-level totals without the instance-type breakdown. Cost and Usage Reports plus QuickSight would give the detail, but you must configure the report, the bucket, the dataset and the dashboards — far more operational overhead.
28:
IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides single sign-on across all accounts in the organization. To keep managing users and groups in the on-premises Active Directory, you use AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a one-way trust, where the AWS domain trusts the corporate domain. That is enough: AWS needs to trust the company, not the other way around.

Why not the others: a two-way trust (B and C) is unnecessary and widens exposure of the corporate directory; C alone also does not deliver SSO across the organization's accounts. Deploying your own on-premises IdP adds work that Identity Center already handles.
51:
Two pieces are needed: a scheduled trigger and an email mechanism that can send HTML. An EventBridge scheduled rule invokes a Lambda function every morning that queries the REST API and builds the report; Amazon SES sends that HTML to several addresses at once.

Why not the others: Kinesis Data Firehose is for streaming ingestion, irrelevant to a daily report. AWS Glue is heavyweight ETL, overkill for calling an API. SNS sends plain text and exposes the subscription address; it cannot format HTML or act as a formatted mailing list.
52:
The output must live in a standard file system structure, scale automatically, be highly available and need minimal operations. Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system that grows elastically into petabytes and spans multiple Availability Zones; mounted from EC2 instances in a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group it satisfies every requirement.

Why not the others: S3 is object storage, not a POSIX file system. EBS is block storage tied to a single AZ and (normally) a single instance, does not scale automatically and cannot be shared across nodes, so neither EKS+EBS nor EC2+EBS qualifies.
53:
The key requirement is that nobody — not administrators, not root — can delete the records for 10 years. Only S3 Object Lock in compliance mode guarantees that (in governance mode a sufficiently privileged user can override it). The records must also be immediately accessible for 1 year and archived for 9 more: a lifecycle rule to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after year one gives the lowest cost with maximum resiliency, since Deep Archive replicates across multiple AZs.

Why not the others: A fails the immediate-access year and an access policy can be edited. B relies on an IAM policy, which root can change. D uses governance mode (overridable) and One Zone-IA, which lives in a single AZ and lacks the maximum resiliency required.
54:
Users already reach the data through Windows file shares (SMB). Amazon FSx for Windows File Server speaks exactly that protocol, integrates with Active Directory, and offers a managed Multi-AZ deployment — so the way users access files is preserved and the manual sync between the two EC2 instances disappears.

Why not the others: moving everything to S3 with IAM authentication completely changes how files are accessed. An S3 File Gateway is meant for on-premises access and still depends on the EC2 instances. EFS only speaks NFS, which is not the native protocol for Windows clients.
55:
Access control between tiers inside a VPC is done with security groups referencing each other. Create a security group for the databases that allows inbound traffic only from the security group attached to the private-subnet instances; only those EC2 instances can then reach RDS, regardless of IP addresses.

Why not the others: security groups do not support deny rules, so B is not possible. Removing routes achieves nothing here, because the local route inside a VPC always exists and cannot be deleted. Peering connects VPCs, not subnets within the same VPC.
56:
To serve a custom domain over HTTPS from API Gateway you need a custom domain name backed by an ACM certificate. For a Regional endpoint, the certificate must be imported into ACM in the same Region as the API (ca-central-1) and attached to the custom domain; Route 53 then points an alias record at that API Gateway domain.

Why not the others: stage variables do not change the public URL or handle certificates. us-east-1 is only required for Edge-optimized endpoints, which use CloudFront, not for Regional ones. An A record pointing at the company's own domain name (D) is circular and will not resolve.
57:
Amazon Rekognition ships with pretrained content moderation for images: it detects nudity, violence and other inappropriate content with a single API call and integrates with Amazon A2I for human review of low-confidence predictions. That is the least development effort.

Why not the others: Comprehend analyzes text, not images. SageMaker and a custom model on Fargate both require training, deploying and maintaining a model — the opposite of minimizing development.
58:
The company wants containers without provisioning or managing the underlying infrastructure. AWS Fargate is the serverless compute engine for containers: you define the task and AWS supplies and patches the servers. ECS on Fargate matches the requirement exactly.

Why not the others: EC2 with Docker, ECS on EC2 worker nodes, and ECS-optimized AMIs all leave patching, scaling and capacity management to the company.
59:
For tens of TB of clickstream per day the canonical pattern is Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion, Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver into an S3 data lake without managing servers, and Redshift for analysis over the aggregate. Everything is managed and scales.

Why not the others: Data Pipeline with EMR is a legacy batch flow with far more operations. An EC2 Auto Scaling group means building and maintaining the ingestion tier yourself. CloudFront is a delivery CDN, not a clickstream ingestion mechanism at that scale.
60:
An Application Load Balancer supports listener rules with a redirect action: on the HTTP listener (port 80) configure a 301 redirect to HTTPS (port 443). It is native, with no code and no application changes.

Why not the others: a network ACL blocking HTTP drops the connection instead of redirecting it, so users see an error. "Replacing HTTP with HTTPS in the URL" is not an actual AWS feature. An NLB operates at layer 4 and cannot perform HTTP redirects.
61:
AWS Secrets Manager is purpose-built for database credentials: it stores them encrypted and provides built-in automatic rotation integrated with RDS through a managed Lambda function. The application retrieves the secret at runtime using the EC2 instance role, so nothing is hardcoded.

Why not the others: instance metadata and an S3 config file require building and maintaining rotation yourself. Parameter Store (standard tier) stores encrypted parameters but has no native automatic rotation — you would have to write it.
62:
The certificate is issued by an external CA, so ACM cannot renew it automatically: managed renewal only applies to certificates ACM itself issues. The correct approach is to import the external certificate into ACM, attach it to the ALB, and set up a notification (EventBridge on the ACM expiration event) to rotate it manually each year.

Why not the others: A and C have ACM or ACM Private CA issue the certificate, contradicting the external-CA requirement. In B, managed renewal does not work with imported key material.
63:
The event-driven serverless pattern is the cheapest and most scalable: .pdf files are uploaded to S3, the PUT event invokes a Lambda function that converts the file and writes the .jpg back to S3. You pay only per conversion and it scales with demand automatically.

Why not the others: DynamoDB is not for storing 5 MB files (its item limit is 400 KB). The Elastic Beanstalk options keep EC2 instances and block storage running, which is far more expensive and operationally heavier for a bursty workload.
64:
Low-latency access to the same data is needed both from AWS and on premises, without changing Windows (SMB) access patterns. The combination is FSx for Windows File Server in AWS as the primary store plus an Amazon FSx File Gateway on premises, which caches frequently accessed data locally and keeps latency low for local users.

Why not the others: A leaves on-premises users reaching AWS over the VPN, with high latency. B and C use S3 File Gateway, an object-oriented path that forces workloads to be reconfigured; B is also not a valid home for the master copy of the data.
65:
The reports are PDF and JPEG, so the text must be extracted first: Amazon Textract does that for documents and scanned images. Then Amazon Comprehend Medical is the pretrained service that identifies protected health information (PHI) in clinical text. Both are managed APIs with no model training.

Why not the others: custom Python libraries and SageMaker mean building and maintaining models. Rekognition can detect text in images but does not extract document text with Textract's fidelity, particularly from PDFs.
66:
The files must be immediately available for the full 4 years and are rarely accessed after the first 30 days. S3 Standard-IA delivers millisecond access at a lower storage price, is multi-AZ (the data is critical and hard to reproduce) and handles 5 MB objects without meaningful penalty. The lifecycle rule transitions to Standard-IA at 30 days and deletes at 4 years.

Why not the others: Glacier does not provide immediate access. One Zone-IA lives in a single AZ, insufficient for critical data. D never deletes the data at 4 years as policy requires — it only archives it.
67:
If the queue has no duplicates but the table does, the message is becoming visible again before the consumer finishes processing and deleting it: the visibility timeout is shorter than the processing time, so another consumer picks up the same message. Increasing the visibility timeout with ChangeMessageVisibility fixes it.

Why not the others: creating a new queue changes nothing. AddPermission manages permissions. The ReceiveMessage wait time controls long polling, which reduces empty responses but does not prevent reprocessing.
68:
The requirement is low, consistent latency (that points to Direct Connect) with high availability at minimum cost, accepting a slower backup. A Direct Connect connection as primary with a Site-to-Site VPN as backup is the standard pattern and the cheapest option that still provides redundancy.

Why not the others: two VPN tunnels cannot deliver consistent latency because they traverse the internet. Two Direct Connect connections give better resiliency but cost far more than needed. There is no Direct Connect "failover attribute" that automatically creates backup connections.
69:
High availability with the least operational effort: spread the Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones and convert the Aurora database to Multi-AZ, which replicates synchronously and fails over automatically with minimal data loss. RDS Proxy pools connections and speeds up failover from the application's perspective.

Why not the others: the multi-Region design (A) is far more complex than HA requires. A single AZ with hourly snapshots means downtime and data loss. Writing to S3 and loading via Lambda (D) is a detour that breaks transactional consistency.
70:
A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and does not interpret HTTP status codes, which is why it never sees the application errors. Replacing it with an Application Load Balancer enables HTTP health checks against an application URL; the Auto Scaling group, using those ELB health checks, then replaces unhealthy instances automatically — no custom scripts.

Why not the others: the NLB cannot perform the URL-based HTTP health checking the application diagnosis needs. The cron job is custom code to maintain. The NLB's UnhealthyHostCount metric would still be based on TCP checks, which never observe the HTTP error.
71:
DynamoDB point-in-time recovery (PITR) maintains continuous backups for the last 35 days and lets you restore to any second, so the effective RPO is seconds — well under 15 minutes — and restoring the table fits inside a 1-hour RTO. It also protects against exactly the stated scenario: data corruption.

Why not the others: global tables replicate the corruption to the other Regions instead of protecting against it. A daily export to Glacier gives a 24-hour RPO and a very slow restore. EBS snapshots do not apply to DynamoDB.
72:
Traffic from the VPC to S3 leaves through the NAT gateway or internet gateway and incurs data transfer charges. An S3 VPC gateway endpoint routes that traffic over the AWS private network with no charge for the endpoint or for in-Region transfer, and the endpoint policy restricts which buckets can be reached.

Why not the others: API Gateway is not an S3 proxy for this case. A NAT gateway is precisely the cost being eliminated and does not accept endpoint policies. Putting the application in a public subnet behind an IGW keeps the internet path and its charges.
73:
The bastion is reached from the corporate network across the internet, so its security group must allow inbound access only from the company's external (public) IP range. The application instances sit in the private subnet, and traffic from the bastion stays inside the VPC, so it arrives with the bastion's private IP: their security group must allow SSH only from that private address.

Why not the others: allowing inbound to the bastion from the application instances reverses the flow. The company's internal range is not what AWS sees when traffic crosses the internet (it is NATed to public IPs). Using the bastion's public IP as the source fails because inside the VPC the traffic keeps its private IP.
74:
The web tier is public and serves HTTPS, so its security group must allow inbound port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. SQL Server listens on port 1433 and should only accept connections from the web tier: the best practice is to allow inbound 1433 referencing the web tier's security group rather than an IP range.

Why not the others: security groups are stateful, so responses return automatically and no matching outbound rules are needed (B and D). Allowing inbound 443 on the database tier (E) is an unnecessary permission that violates least privilege.
75:
The problem is that transactions are dropped when a tier is overloaded, so the tiers must be decoupled by a buffer that absorbs spikes. The most modern, lowest-operations answer is API Gateway plus Lambda as the application layer (no servers to manage) with SQS as the communication layer between services, holding messages until they can be processed.

Why not the others: enlarging the EC2 instances modernizes nothing and fails again at the next peak. SNS is publish/subscribe with no per-consumer persistence and no "queue length". D does decouple, but keeps EC2 and scales reactively on failures, with more overhead than the serverless option.
76:
AWS DataSync is built to move large volumes of files (the JSON on the SAN) into S3 as a managed service, with integrity validation, retries and encryption in transit. Running it over AWS Direct Connect provides dedicated bandwidth and predictable throughput, which makes the transfer more reliable and keeps the sensitive data off the public internet.

Why not the others: DataSync over the public internet is less reliable and less predictable. DMS migrates databases, not JSON files sitting on a SAN.
77:
Three pieces are required with minimal overhead: API Gateway as a fully managed API, Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion, and Kinesis Data Firehose — with Lambda transformation — to deliver the transformed data into S3. Nothing to administer.

Why not the others: A and B host the API on an EC2 instance that must be patched and scaled. AWS Glue is batch/micro-batch ETL, not a real-time streaming delivery service like Firehose.
78:
AWS Backup supports DynamoDB natively and lets you define plans with schedules and long-term retention policies (the 7 years) centrally, with cold storage. It is the least operational option.

Why not the others: PITR only retains 35 days, far short of 7 years. On-demand backups from the console are manual and are not managed through S3 lifecycle as described. Building the backup with EventBridge and Lambda is custom code to maintain.
79:
Traffic is idle most mornings and spiky and unpredictable in the evenings, with spikes arriving very quickly. On-demand capacity mode charges per request, costs nothing when the table is idle, and absorbs sudden spikes instantly with no capacity planning.

Why not the others: a global secondary index changes query patterns, not cost behavior. Provisioned capacity with auto scaling reacts in minutes, so very fast spikes get throttled, and you keep paying for baseline capacity during idle mornings. A global table multiplies cost for a replication requirement nobody asked for.
81:
Durable job storage plus loose coupling points to Amazon SQS, which persists each job until a worker deletes it. The Auto Scaling group should scale on the queue depth — the number of items waiting — because that is the real measure of pending work. Launch templates are the current, recommended alternative to launch configurations.

Why not the others: SNS does not durably store jobs; subscribers that are absent simply miss the message. Scaling on CPU or network usage is an indirect proxy that does not reflect the backlog.
82:
ACM emits an ACM Certificate Approaching Expiration event to EventBridge daily, starting 45 days before expiry, for both issued and imported certificates. An EventBridge rule can filter on 30 days remaining and invoke a Lambda function that publishes a custom alert to SNS.

Why not the others: ACM has no built-in rule engine to publish custom SNS messages on a schedule. The AWS Config approach works but adds a rule, evaluations and extra cost for something EventBridge already emits. Trusted Advisor's certificate check requires a Business or Enterprise support plan and offers less precise control.
83:
The backend must stay on the on-premises servers in the United States and the launch is days away, so nothing can be migrated. Amazon CloudFront accepts a custom origin — including servers outside AWS — and immediately puts edge locations across Europe in front of them, cutting latency for the new users and carrying traffic over the AWS backbone. It is a configuration change, not a migration.

Why not the others: launching an EC2 instance in us-east-1 and migrating the site contradicts keeping the backend on premises and takes time. S3 with Cross-Region Replication only serves static content, and the site is dynamic. Route 53 geoproximity routing still sends every European request all the way to the US servers.
84:
Production runs 24 hours a day, which is exactly the steady baseline Reserved Instances are designed for and where the discount is largest. Development and test run at least 8 hours a day and will be stopped automatically when idle, so On-Demand — billed only while running — is the cheapest fit for them.

Why not the others: Spot Instances for production risk interruption of a live environment. Reserved Instances for development and test would be paid for around the clock even while the instances are stopped, wasting the commitment. Spot blocks are no longer offered and would not suit predictable dev/test hours.
85:
New documents must not be modified or deleted after they are stored — that is WORM, and S3 Object Lock is the feature that enforces it. Object Lock requires versioning to be enabled on the bucket, so both are turned on together.

Why not the others: a lifecycle policy only moves data between storage classes. Versioning with a read-only ACL still lets a privileged user delete or overwrite, and permissions can be changed. EFS mounted read-only only restricts that mount; the data itself remains mutable.
86:
AWS Secrets Manager stores database credentials encrypted and rotates them automatically on a schedule using a managed Lambda rotation function tied to RDS. The web servers retrieve the secret at runtime with IAM permissions granted to their instance role, so the connection is secure and the frequent-rotation requirement is met natively.

Why not the others: Systems Manager OpsCenter is for operational issue tracking, not secrets. An S3 bucket or KMS-encrypted files on the file system store credentials but leave rotation entirely up to you to build.
87:
Customer data is lost because the write path is synchronous and the database is temporarily unavailable. Putting the data in an SQS queue decouples ingestion from persistence: the API keeps accepting records during the upgrade, and a separate Lambda function drains the queue into the database once it is back. A FIFO queue additionally preserves the order of the customer events.

Why not the others: RDS Proxy helps with connection pooling and failover but cannot buffer writes while the database is being upgraded. Longer timeouts and retries still fail if the upgrade outlasts the maximum 15-minute Lambda run. Lambda local storage is ephemeral and not shared between invocations, so the data can vanish.
88:
With S3 Requester Pays, the requester — the European marketing firm — pays the request and data transfer charges instead of the bucket owner; the owner still pays only for storage. That directly minimizes the company's transfer costs for 3 TB of shared data.

Why not the others: Cross-Region Replication makes the company pay for the transfer and for a second copy. Plain cross-account access leaves the transfer charges with the bucket owner. Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage cost, not transfer, and syncing buckets adds transfer cost.
89:
The concern is accidental deletion. S3 Versioning keeps every version, so a delete only adds a delete marker and the object can be recovered. MFA Delete adds a second factor before anyone can permanently delete a version or disable versioning — the stronger protection managers are asking for.

Why not the others: MFA on user sign-in does not protect the objects once a user is authenticated. Lifecycle policies are not attached to IAM users and cannot deny actions. Encrypting with KMS and blocking key access prevents reading, not deleting.
90:
The reporting script's read queries are competing with development traffic on a single instance. Creating a read replica and pointing the script at it moves that read load off the primary; it is a managed feature with no code to write.

Why not the others: a Multi-AZ standby does not serve read traffic, so it does not relieve the load. Manual daily exports add work and break the requirement to report during business hours. ElastiCache requires application changes and does not help queries that run at random intervals over changing data.
91:
An S3 gateway endpoint gives instances in the VPC a private route to S3 through the AWS network. Traffic never traverses the internet and there is no need for an internet gateway or NAT.

Why not the others: S3 buckets are not created inside subnets, so B is not a real option. Being in the same Region does not by itself keep traffic off the internet. A NAT gateway is exactly the internet path that the security regulation forbids.
92:
Two things are needed: a private network path and a least-privilege access policy. A VPC gateway endpoint for S3 keeps the traffic inside the AWS network, and a bucket policy scoped to that endpoint / the application tier ensures only those EC2 instances can reach the data.

Why not the others: making the objects public directly contradicts storing sensitive user information. Copying long-lived IAM user credentials onto an instance is an anti-pattern — use an instance role. A NAT instance sends traffic over the internet and is more to manage.
93:
Aurora database cloning creates a copy of the production database in minutes using copy-on-write, without any data movement, so the staging environment is ready almost instantly and production takes no load or latency hit. Aurora Replicas across AZs cover the heavy read activity and availability requirement.

Why not the others: any mysqldump-based export/restore (A and D) reproduces the exact latency problem and the long wait the team already suffers. In C, the Multi-AZ standby cannot be used as a staging database — it is not accessible for reads or writes.
94:
S3 event notifications into an SQS queue, consumed by a Lambda function, gives near-immediate per-file processing that scales from zero to thousands of files with no servers. Storing the JSON output in DynamoDB keeps the whole path serverless.

Why not the others: EMR is a batch cluster, heavy and slow to react to single small files. EC2 consumers must be provisioned, patched and scaled even on days with no uploads. D adds Kinesis Data Streams — a shard-based service to manage — for an event S3 can deliver directly.
95:
Read replicas offload read traffic from the primary and require no application redesign beyond pointing reads at the replica endpoint. The replicas should match the source instance's compute and storage so they can keep up with the replication stream and serve the read volume without becoming the new bottleneck.

Why not the others: in a Multi-AZ deployment the standby serves no traffic, so neither A nor B separates reads from writes. Undersized replicas (C) fall behind in replication lag and degrade performance.
97:
SharePoint needs Windows shared file storage over SMB with Active Directory access control. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server provides native SMB, AD integration and a Multi-AZ highly available deployment as a fully managed service.

Why not the others: EFS is NFS and does not authenticate against Active Directory in this way. A Storage Gateway file gateway is designed for hybrid access, not as the primary highly available store for this workload. S3 cannot be mounted as a native Windows volume for SharePoint.
98:
With an SQS queue as a Lambda event source, the message must stay invisible for as long as the function may take to process it. If the visibility timeout is shorter than the function timeout plus the batch window, the message becomes visible again and is delivered a second time — hence the duplicate emails. Setting the visibility timeout above that total (AWS recommends about 6x the function timeout) fixes it with a single setting change.

Why not the others: long polling reduces empty receives, not duplicates. Switching to FIFO means recreating the queue and reconfiguring the pipeline, and S3 event notifications do not supply deduplication IDs. Deleting the message before processing loses data whenever the function fails.
99:
The requirement names Lustre clients explicitly and demands a fully managed service. Amazon FSx for Lustre is the managed, high-performance Lustre file system, and it can be accessed from on premises over Direct Connect or VPN.

Why not the others: Storage Gateway offers NFS and SMB, not Lustre. Building a Windows file share on EC2 is neither Lustre nor managed. EFS is NFS only and cannot be configured to support Lustre.
100:
AWS KMS is the managed service for encryption and decryption operations in near real time: create a customer managed key, allow the EC2 instance role to use it, and store the resulting ciphertext in Amazon S3, which is highly available and durable by design (11 nines) across multiple AZs.

Why not the others: Secrets Manager with manual certificate updates adds ongoing toil. A custom Lambda with a crypto library means writing and maintaining your own encryption code. EBS volumes are tied to a single AZ, so they do not meet the highly available storage requirement as well as S3.
101:
A NAT gateway lives in a public subnet and is a zonal resource. For high availability you deploy one NAT gateway per Availability Zone and give each AZ's private subnet its own route table pointing at the local NAT gateway — so a single AZ failure cannot cut internet access for the others (and it avoids cross-AZ data charges).

Why not the others: NAT instances are self-managed EC2 and go in public subnets, not private ones. A VPC can have only one internet gateway attached, and putting one on a private subnet would make it public. An egress-only internet gateway is IPv6-only, while this VPC uses IPv4.
102:
AWS DataSync automates the transfer: you deploy a DataSync agent in the on-premises data center to read the NFS-based file system and configure the EFS file system as the destination. Launching the EC2 instance in the same Availability Zone as the EFS mount target keeps latency low and avoids cross-AZ data charges.

Why not the others: a secondary EBS volume contradicts the requirement to use EFS. Copying with an OS command is manual, which is exactly what must be automated. DataSync does not support SFTP as a location type — the source is the NFS file system.
103:
AWS Glue job bookmarks track state between runs, recording which data has already been processed so subsequent runs only handle new files. That is the built-in answer to reprocessing.

Why not the others: deleting processed data destroys the source and may break other consumers. NumberOfWorkers controls parallelism and only makes the job slower. FindMatches is an ML transform for record deduplication and entity matching, unrelated to incremental processing.
104:
AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced DDoS protection with 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team and cost protection for scaling during an attack. Serving the site through Amazon CloudFront — for both static and dynamic content — absorbs and disperses the attack across the global edge network, keeping the origin protected. That combination handles a large, distributed attack without downtime.

Why not the others: GuardDuty detects and reports threats but does not block traffic. A Lambda function updating network ACLs cannot keep up with thousands of IPs and NACLs have rule limits. Spot Instances with autoscaling only scales up to absorb the flood — expensive, interruptible and not mitigation.
105:
EventBridge invokes the function, so EventBridge needs permission to call it. That permission belongs in a resource-based policy on the Lambda function granting lambda:InvokeFunction to the events.amazonaws.com service principal — the narrowest possible grant.

Why not the others: an execution role defines what the function itself may do to other services, not who may invoke it. Using * as the principal lets anyone invoke it. Granting lambda:* is far broader than the single needed action.
106:
SSE-KMS gives encryption at rest with keys managed in AWS KMS; every key usage is logged to CloudTrail, satisfying the auditing requirement. Enabling automatic rotation makes KMS rotate the key material yearly with no work at all — the most operationally efficient answer.

Why not the others: SSE-C makes you manage and supply keys with every request. SSE-S3 does not log individual key usage or let you control rotation. Manual rotation of a KMS key meets the requirement but adds recurring operational work.
107:
The location data points arrive continuously during peak hours and must be usable by the existing analytics platform and reachable through a REST API. Amazon API Gateway exposes the REST interface, and Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics processes the streaming location data in real time before feeding the analytics platform.

Why not the others: Athena over S3 queries data at rest, not a live stream. API Gateway with Lambda alone provides the API but no storage or analytics tier. QuickSight with Redshift is a BI/warehouse combination that does not expose a REST API for the data points.
108:
The data must reach multiple target systems, which is the classic fan-out pattern: an SNS topic with multiple SQS queues subscribed, one per target, so each target gets its own durable copy and consumes at its own pace. RDS event notifications integrate directly with SNS.

Why not the others: sending to a single SQS queue (A and B) means only one consumer receives each message — no fan-out. C inverts the pattern; SQS cannot fan out into SNS topics.
109:
The retention period is not known in advance — the objects stay immutable until the company decides otherwise. That is exactly what an S3 Object Lock legal hold does: it protects an object version indefinitely with no retention date, and it can be removed later. Only users granted s3:PutObjectLegalHold can lift it and delete the objects. Object Lock requires versioning.

Why not the others: a Glacier vault lock is permanent and cannot be modified once locked. A 100-year retention period is a fixed term, not the open-ended behavior described. CloudTrail plus restores is detective, not preventive.
110:
The slowdown comes from resizing the image synchronously inside the upload request. The fix is to take the resize off that path: the web server simply stores the original image in S3, and an S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function that resizes it afterwards. The upload returns as soon as the object lands, and the two responsibilities are decoupled.

Why not the others: uploading to S3 Glacier makes retrieval slow and is unrelated to the problem. A presigned-URL upload straight from the browser (C) also removes work from the web tier and is a valid pattern, but it changes the client application rather than the server-side coupling this question targets. A scheduled Lambda batch (E) adds latency instead of processing each image on arrival.
111:
Highest availability means removing every single point of failure and letting AWS manage the pieces. Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers across two AZs replaces the self-managed ActiveMQ instance, an Auto Scaling group spanning two AZs replaces the consumer instances (so a failed instance is automatically replaced, not just duplicated), and RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ handles database failover.

Why not the others: A keeps everything self-managed, with the highest operational complexity. B and C stop short — B still self-manages MySQL replication, and C uses fixed consumer instances that are never replaced when one fails.
112:
The application is already containerized, so ECS on AWS Fargate runs it with no code changes and no servers to manage; Service Auto Scaling handles the growing request volume and an Application Load Balancer distributes traffic.

Why not the others: two fixed EC2 instances do not scale and must be patched. Rewriting the app as Lambda functions is exactly the development effort the company wants to avoid. AWS ParallelCluster targets HPC batch workloads, not a request-serving web application.
113:
There is no spare network bandwidth, so any online transfer is out; 50 TB fits an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device. Once the data lands in S3, AWS Glue is the serverless, managed way to run the weekly transformation in the cloud, which is the least operational overhead.

Why not the others: DataSync needs the bandwidth the data center does not have. Snowcone holds only 8-14 TB, far short of 50 TB. Running the custom application on an EC2 instance (D) means maintaining a server and the legacy code instead of using a managed ETL service.
114:
Concurrency varies sharply by time of day, so the compute must scale to zero and back automatically: AWS Lambda processes each photo on upload. The photos themselves belong in Amazon S3, which scales without limit and is far cheaper for binary objects, while DynamoDB continues to hold the metadata it already stores.

Why not the others: DynamoDB cannot store photos (400 KB item limit). Kinesis Data Firehose is a delivery stream for streaming data, not an image processor. Three fixed EC2 instances with io2 volumes neither scale elastically nor store images cost-effectively.
115:
The requirement is a private path to S3. Moving the instances into private subnets removes their direct internet exposure, and an S3 gateway VPC endpoint associated with the private route table sends the file transfers over the AWS private network.

Why not the others: a NAT gateway still routes through the internet gateway. Restricting outbound traffic to the S3 prefix list controls where traffic can go but it still travels over the internet. Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS, which is not the situation here.
116:
The site is static and changes only four times a year, so host it in an S3 bucket with static website hosting — nothing to patch and effectively unlimited scale. Putting Amazon CloudFront in front adds HTTPS, caching at the edge and a security boundary in front of the bucket.

Why not the others: AWS WAF filters requests but does not provide HTTPS termination. A Lambda function serving the content is unnecessary custom code for static files. An Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances behind an ALB reintroduces exactly the patching burden the company wants to escape.
117:
A CloudWatch Logs log group can be configured as a source for a Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream with Amazon OpenSearch Service as its destination. Firehose is fully managed, buffers and delivers in near real time, and handles retries and index rotation without any code.

Why not the others: (Note that a native CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to OpenSearch also exists and is a common answer to this question; the study key selects the Firehose delivery stream.) Writing a Lambda function to ship the logs is custom code to maintain. Installing Kinesis Agent on every server is a large amount of per-host configuration and bypasses the logs already in CloudWatch.
118:
900 TB of text documents accessed by web servers across multiple AZs, with cost as a concern, points to Amazon S3: unlimited elastic capacity, no provisioning, high durability and by far the lowest price per GB, accessible over HTTP from any instance.

Why not the others: EBS volumes are AZ-bound, capped in size and would need provisioning and replication. EFS works across AZs but costs several times more per GB at this scale. OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, not a document store for 900 TB of files.
119:
AWS WAF is the service that blocks SQL injection and cross-site scripting, and it integrates directly with API Gateway through a Regional web ACL associated with an API stage. Web ACLs are Regional resources, so one is needed in us-east-1 and one in ap-southeast-2.

Why not the others: (Firewall Manager centralizes WAF rules across accounts and is often cited for multi-account setups; the study key selects the direct WAF association.) AWS Shield protects against DDoS, not injection attacks, and does not use web ACLs on its own, so neither C nor D works.
120:
Route 53 geolocation routing sends users in the United States to the us-west-2 NLB and users in Europe to the eu-west-1 NLB, so requests reach the nearest set of instances; fronting the Route 53 record with a CloudFront distribution brings the connection onto the AWS edge network for faster and more consistent performance.

Why not the others: (AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups in both Regions is the pattern most often cited for NLB-backed workloads and is worth knowing; the study key selects the Route 53 answer.) Attaching Elastic IPs to all six instances discards the load balancers and their health checking. Replacing the NLBs with ALBs is an unnecessary rebuild for a DNS workload.
121:
You cannot turn on encryption for an existing unencrypted RDS instance. The supported path is to take a snapshot, copy the snapshot while enabling encryption, restore a new DB instance from that encrypted copy and cut over to it. From then on the instance and all its snapshots are encrypted.

Why not the others: RDS storage is not managed through your own EBS volumes, and encryption cannot simply be switched on. You cannot restore an encrypted snapshot into an existing unencrypted instance. Copying snapshots to an encrypted S3 bucket does nothing for the live database.
122:
AWS KMS is the managed key management service: it creates, stores, rotates and controls access to encryption keys, integrates with the AWS SDKs and most AWS services, and logs every use to CloudTrail. Developers get a scalable key infrastructure with no hardware or software to operate.

Why not the others: MFA and IAM policies control access to keys but do not provide key management infrastructure. ACM issues and manages TLS certificates, not general-purpose data encryption keys.
123:
SSL termination is consuming the web servers' CPU. Moving termination to an Application Load Balancer offloads it entirely: import the company's existing certificate into AWS Certificate Manager and attach it to an HTTPS listener on the ALB. The instances then serve plain HTTP and regain their capacity, and the ALB adds distribution and health checks.

Why not the others: ACM cannot issue a certificate for a domain the company controls without validation and, more importantly, keeping termination on the instances does not solve the CPU problem — and ACM certificates cannot be installed on EC2. Storing a certificate in S3 does nothing. A single proxy EC2 instance just moves the bottleneck and adds a single point of failure.
124:
The job is stateless, can be interrupted at any time with no negative impact, and is highly dynamic — the textbook profile for EC2 Spot Instances, which cost up to 90% less than On-Demand.

Why not the others: Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment for a steady baseline the job does not have. On-Demand works but costs far more for an interruption-tolerant workload. Lambda cannot run the job because it takes over 60 minutes, beyond the 15-minute maximum.
125:
Nothing may be exposed to the public internet except the load balancer, and the instances still need outbound internet access for the payment provider. So: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group in private subnets with a Multi-AZ RDS instance also in private subnets, inside a VPC with two public subnets (for the Application Load Balancer), two private subnets and a NAT gateway in each AZ for outbound access and high availability.

Why not the others: an internet-facing ALB cannot live in private subnets. Launching the EC2 instances in public subnets exposes them, violating the requirement. A design with a single public and single private subnet cannot be highly available across two AZs.
126:
Data from the last 2 years must be highly available and immediately retrievable, so it stays in S3 Standard. Everything older can be archived at the lowest possible cost for the remaining 23 years, which is S3 Glacier Deep Archive. A lifecycle policy that transitions objects after 2 years does exactly that.

Why not the others: transitioning immediately breaks the immediate-retrieval requirement for recent data. Intelligent-Tiering's archive tiers move objects based on access patterns, which does not guarantee the 2-year availability rule. One Zone-IA sacrifices availability by keeping only one AZ copy.
127:
Three distinct needs, three services: Amazon EBS (io2/io2 Block Express) delivers the maximum I/O performance for the 10 TB of video processing volumes; Amazon S3 provides 11 nines of durability for the 300 TB of media content; and S3 Glacier is the low-cost archive for the 900 TB no longer in use.

Why not the others: EFS is a shared file system but not the maximum-performance block option. The EC2 instance store is ephemeral — data is lost when the instance stops — so it cannot hold the working video data reliably, and S3 Standard would be an expensive archive tier.
129:
The pain is operational overhead and capacity planning. Moving the containers to AWS Fargate with Amazon ECS eliminates host management and capacity planning entirely, and migrating PostgreSQL to Amazon Aurora hands off patching, backups, replication and failover to AWS while improving performance.

Why not the others: hosting the containers on EC2 keeps the servers the company is trying to stop maintaining. CloudFront and ElastiCache are performance optimizations that do nothing about the infrastructure burden described.
130:
A target tracking scaling policy takes a metric and a target value — here average CPU utilization at 40% — and Auto Scaling adds or removes instances automatically to hold the group near that number, like a thermostat.

Why not the others: simple scaling reacts to a single alarm with a fixed adjustment and a cooldown, which is coarser and slower. A Lambda function updating desired capacity is custom code duplicating a built-in feature. Scheduled scaling assumes a predictable time pattern, which is not the requirement here.
131:
An origin access identity (OAI) is a special CloudFront principal; you grant read permission on the bucket to only that OAI and remove public access. CloudFront can then fetch the objects while direct requests to the S3 URL are denied. (In current AWS documentation this pattern has been superseded by origin access control, or OAC, which works the same way.)

Why not the others: writing per-bucket policies without an identity to grant to does not actually block direct access. IAM users are not assignable to a CloudFront distribution. A distribution ID is not a valid principal in a bucket policy.
132:
The files are static downloadable reports served to a global audience. Storing them in Amazon S3 and distributing them through Amazon CloudFront gives edge caching close to every user for the fastest response, provisions no infrastructure, and costs the least.

Why not the others: Lambda with DynamoDB is for dynamic API workloads, not file downloads. An ALB with EC2 Auto Scaling provisions servers in a single Region and serves distant users slowly. Route 53 with internal load balancers does not even expose the content publicly.
133:
The company needs access to the underlying operating system of the database host, which rules out standard RDS, and wants minimal operational overhead, which rules out plain EC2. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle is the middle ground: a managed RDS experience that still grants OS and database privileges. A cross-Region read replica provides the disaster recovery setup with little effort.

Why not the others: self-managing Oracle on EC2 with your own replication is the highest overhead. Standard RDS for Oracle (B and D) does not give operating system access, and a standby in another AZ is high availability, not cross-Region DR.
134:
Amazon Athena queries data directly in S3 with standard SQL and is serverless, so it covers both existing and new data with no infrastructure. The encryption and replication requirements are met with SSE-KMS using multi-Region keys, which lets the replica Region decrypt the replicated objects with the same key without cross-Region key calls. Loading into a new bucket lets you apply the encryption configuration cleanly from the start.

Why not the others: Amazon RDS is not serverless SQL over S3 and would require loading the data into a database. SSE-S3 works but does not offer the multi-Region key control this design calls for.
135:
AWS PrivateLink is exactly this scenario: the provider exposes its service through a VPC endpoint service, and the company creates an interface endpoint in its own VPC. Traffic stays on the AWS private network, is restricted to that single target service, and connections can only be initiated from the consumer side.

Why not the others: VPC peering opens full network reachability in both directions, far broader than one service. A NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet. A virtual private gateway is for VPN connections to on-premises networks, not for exposing a service.
136:
The source database must stay online and the two must remain in sync, so AWS DMS is the tool: you provision a DMS replication instance and create a task with ongoing replication (change data capture) so changes keep flowing after the initial full load. Because this is a heterogeneous-style migration to Aurora PostgreSQL, the AWS Schema Conversion Tool prepares the schema first.

Why not the others: a one-time backup gives a point-in-time copy that immediately goes stale. An EventBridge rule to monitor synchronization is optional observability, not a step that performs the migration.
137:
The root user email address should be a distribution list reaching a small group of administrators rather than a single person, so a missed message is not possible. In addition, AWS Organizations lets you set alternate contacts (billing, operations, security) per account, ensuring notifications reach the right administrators. That combination keeps notifications limited to account administrators.

Why not the others: (Note the study key marks the option that reuses one root email address across all accounts; in practice each AWS account requires a unique root email, so the distribution-list answer is the technically sound one.) Forwarding root email to every user in the organization broadcasts sensitive notifications far too widely, and routing everything through a single administrator recreates the same single point of failure.
138:
Highest availability with least operational overhead means replacing each self-managed component with a managed, multi-AZ one: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ in an active/standby pair across AZs, a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group for the processing application, and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with Multi-AZ for the database.

Why not the others: A leaves PostgreSQL running on self-managed EC2 in an Auto Scaling group, which does not give a coherent database failover story. C and D keep RabbitMQ self-managed on EC2, and an Auto Scaling group does not make a message broker highly available on its own.
139:
S3 replication copies objects between buckets automatically, without any Lambda code to write or maintain. However, S3 event notifications support only a limited set of destinations (SNS, SQS, Lambda), so to fan out to both a Lambda function and SageMaker Pipelines you route the analysis bucket's events through Amazon EventBridge, where a single ObjectCreated rule can have multiple targets.

Why not the others: (The study key selects the option that copies with a Lambda function; note that S3 replication removes that custom code, which is why option D is frequently cited as the lowest-overhead answer.) The options using plain S3 event notifications cannot target SageMaker Pipelines directly.
140:
The ingestion layer on EC2 is sporadic, unpredictable and interruption-tolerant — the exact profile for Spot Instances. The Fargate front end and the Lambda API layer have predictable utilization over the next year, and a Compute Savings Plan is the only commitment type that covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda together.

Why not the others: On-Demand for ingestion costs far more than Spot for an interruptible workload. All Upfront Reserved Instances commit to a steady baseline the sporadic ingestion layer does not have. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan applies only to EC2 usage, so it would not cover Fargate or Lambda.
141:
The content is heavily personalized per user, so caching gives limited benefit; running the full stack in two AWS Regions and using a Route 53 latency routing policy sends each user to the Region that answers fastest for them, shortening the round trip for dynamic requests worldwide.

Why not the others: (Fronting a single-Region ALB with CloudFront, option A, is also a very common answer to this question, because CloudFront accelerates dynamic content over the AWS backbone; the study key selects the two-Region design.) Serving dynamic content straight from a single-Region ALB (C) leaves distant users with the worst latency. Geolocation routing (D) picks by the user's country rather than by measured latency, so it can route to a slower Region.
142:
Three clues point the same way: UDP traffic, static IP addresses for entry, and routing to the nearest edge location. AWS Global Accelerator provides two static anycast IPs, enters the AWS backbone at the closest edge, and supports UDP; it forwards to a Network Load Balancer, which is the layer-4 balancer that handles UDP. The modified Linux kernel means the application must run on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group.

Why not the others: CloudFront and API Gateway are HTTP/HTTPS services and cannot carry UDP. An Application Load Balancer is HTTP-only. Lambda cannot run a modified Linux kernel.
143:
The company wants to keep most of the existing code but split the monolith into smaller applications owned by different teams, with high scalability and low operational overhead. Containerizing the pieces and running them on Amazon ECS behind an Application Load Balancer preserves the code, gives each team its own service, and lets ECS handle scaling and placement.

Why not the others: rewriting for Lambda (A and B) means substantial code changes, and Amplify targets front-end hosting. Plain EC2 instances behind an ALB keep the monolith and add server management.
144:
The reports are read-heavy queries competing with the production workload. An Aurora Replica shares the same storage volume, adds read capacity with almost no lag, and is far cheaper than upsizing the whole cluster. Pointing the monthly reporting at the replica isolates the spike.

Why not the others: Redshift means building and loading a data warehouse for a monthly job. A larger instance class pays for extra capacity 24/7 to serve a monthly peak. Aurora storage scales I/O automatically — you do not provision IOPS on it.
145:
Seamless scaling at the lowest cost means an Auto Scaling group: bake the web application into an AMI, reference it from a launch template, put the group behind an Application Load Balancer, and use Spot capacity for the stateless web tier to cut costs sharply. Moving MySQL onto Aurora removes the database from the instance and gives it a managed, scalable home.

Why not the others: A and B add exactly one more fixed instance — that is not seamless scaling, and Route 53 weighted routing has no health-based elasticity. C scales vertically with downtime every time the instance is resized.
146:
Usage has a steady, always-present baseline (moderate overnight, heavy during the workday) plus a variable component. Reserved Instances cover the baseline at a large discount for capacity that is always running, and Spot Instances absorb the extra demand cheaply — availability is preserved because the baseline is never at risk.

Why not the others: Spot for the entire workload risks interruption of the whole production application. On-Demand for the baseline pays full price for predictable, always-on usage. Dedicated Instances cost more and address hardware isolation, which is not a requirement here.
147:
S3 is the cost-effective home for more than 10 TB of logs per month, and S3 Lifecycle policies are the native, no-cost mechanism to transition objects older than 1 month to S3 Glacier Deep Archive — the cheapest class for rarely accessed data kept 10 years.

Why not the others: AWS Backup does not perform S3 storage class transitions like this. CloudWatch Logs is significantly more expensive at this volume and its retention settings only delete data; S3 Lifecycle policies cannot act on CloudWatch Logs.
148:
The failures are transient, so the answer is to capture what failed and reprocess it. Configuring an SQS queue as the Lambda function's on-failure destination sends every failed invocation's event to the queue, where it is stored durably and can be processed later — nothing is lost and no manual rerun is needed.

Why not the others: Lambda already runs across multiple AZs. More CPU and memory does not fix network connectivity. SNS retries eventually give up and the message is discarded unless a dead-letter queue exists.
149:
Order must be preserved throughout processing, which is the defining feature of an SQS FIFO queue: messages are delivered exactly once and strictly in order within a message group. A Lambda function polling the queue processes them with no servers to manage.

Why not the others: SNS makes no ordering guarantee for standard topics and does not durably queue per consumer. An SQS standard queue is best-effort ordering only. D introduces SNS in front of SQS without solving ordering and adds a component for no benefit.
150:
A CloudWatch composite alarm combines the states of several alarms with a rule such as ALARM(cpu) AND ALARM(readIops). That is exactly the requirement: do not act on a short CPU burst alone, but act when high CPU coincides with high read IOPS — and it reduces false alarms by suppressing individual noisy alarms.

Why not the others: dashboards visualize but do not alarm. Synthetics canaries test application endpoints, not instance metrics. A single metric alarm watches one metric; it cannot express a condition across two metrics.
152:
The database is needed only 12 hours a day, and a stopped RDS instance stops incurring instance-hours. EventBridge scheduled rules invoking small Lambda functions to stop and start the DB instance is the standard, low-cost automation for that.

Why not the others: Session Manager is for shell access to instances and has nothing to do with scheduling RDS. A Redis cache does not let users read data while the database is down in any meaningful way for a training app. Running a dedicated EC2 instance with a cron job adds a server (and its cost) just to run a scheduler.
153:
Objects are at least 128 KB and are rarely downloaded after 90 days, but recent files must stay instantly available. An S3 Lifecycle rule transitioning from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA at 90 days lowers storage cost while keeping millisecond retrieval, and the 128 KB minimum billable size for Standard-IA is already satisfied.

Why not the others: starting objects in Standard-IA penalizes the frequently accessed first 90 days with retrieval charges. Intelligent-Tiering adds a monitoring fee per object across millions of files when the access pattern is already known. S3 Inventory is a reporting feature and cannot move objects.
154:
No user — not even an administrator — may modify or delete files, and each file must be kept at least 1 year from creation. S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 365-day retention period enforces exactly that and cannot be overridden or shortened by anyone. Write access for the few scientists is then granted with ordinary bucket permissions.

Why not the others: governance mode can be bypassed by privileged users, and a legal hold has no time period. IAM roles and bucket policies can be changed by whoever administers them. A Lambda function tracking hashes detects tampering after the fact instead of preventing it.
155:
Amazon CloudFront caches the media at edge locations worldwide, so users everywhere get fast, reliable delivery while the S3 origin sees far less load. For confidential content, CloudFront also supports signed URLs and signed cookies plus origin access control so the bucket stays private.

Why not the others: DataSync moves data between storage systems; it is not a delivery network. Global Accelerator improves network paths to regional endpoints but does not cache content and does not front S3 buckets this way. SQS is a message queue.
156:
Two managed pieces cover the whole pipeline. For ingestion and staging, AWS Lake Formation blueprints identify the sources and orchestrate AWS Glue crawlers and jobs that extract from the databases and land the data in S3 as Apache Parquet — a columnar format built for analytics. For consumption, Amazon Athena runs the one-time SQL queries directly on S3 and Amazon QuickSight builds the KPI dashboards. Nothing to provision.

Why not the others: Kinesis Data Analytics queries streams in flight, not ad-hoc historical data. Custom Lambda functions moving individual records into Redshift is code to write and operate. Loading into multiple OpenSearch clusters adds clusters to run for a BI use case Athena already covers.
158:
Amazon CloudFront accelerates both cases: for live streaming it distributes the segmented HTTP stream from the edge to a global audience, and for the on-demand videos afterwards it caches the files close to viewers. One service covers real-time and on-demand delivery.

Why not the others: Global Accelerator improves TCP/UDP routing to regional endpoints but does not cache media. Route 53 only resolves DNS. S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads into a bucket, not distribution to viewers.
161:
The workload is event-driven and bursty: documents land in S3, and an S3 event invokes a Lambda function that runs the existing Python code. Lambda is inherently highly available and scales from zero to thousands of concurrent executions with no servers, and Aurora provides the managed SQL destination for the results.

Why not the others: A and C keep EC2 instances to size, patch and scale, and EBS Multi-Attach is a niche feature with a strict clustered-file-system requirement. D runs ECS on the EC2 launch type, which still means managing the cluster capacity.
162:
Amazon FSx for Lustre is the high-performance parallel file system for Linux HPC workloads, and it links natively to an Amazon S3 bucket: S3 objects appear as files in the file system, and results can be exported back to S3 for long-term persistence. On-premises data is copied into S3 once, and every EC2 Spot Instance in the cluster mounts the same Lustre file system.

Why not the others: FSx for Windows File Server is SMB for Windows workloads. Glacier is archival, not a working file system. A gp2 EBS volume cannot be shared across hundreds of instances or deliver HPC throughput.
163:
ECR stores the container images, and ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type runs them without any cluster infrastructure to manage — Fargate provisions the compute per task. Target tracking scaling grows and shrinks the service with demand, and tasks spread across Availability Zones for high availability.

Why not the others: the EC2 launch type leaves instance capacity, patching and scaling to the company. Running your own registry and hand-launching EC2 instances is the highest overhead. Baking containers into an AMI defeats the purpose of containers and makes deployments slow.
166:
Millions of global viewers requesting the same static HTML is the canonical CloudFront use case: put a CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket so pages are cached and served from the edge nearest each user, cutting latency and the load and cost on the origin.

Why not the others: presigned URLs restrict access, they do not improve delivery. Replicating the bucket to every Region multiplies storage cost and still requires routing logic. Route 53 geoproximity routes DNS between endpoints you must build yourself in each Region.
167:
The queue is always being processed, so there is a baseline of capacity that runs continuously — cover that with Reserved Instances for the largest discount. The intermittent, unpredictable spikes are handled by Spot Instances, which are cheap and safe here because SQS makes the workers interruption-tolerant: an interrupted message simply becomes visible again.

Why not the others: Spot only for maximum capacity risks losing the whole fleet, breaking the no-downtime requirement. Reserved Instances for peak capacity pays for idle capacity most of the time. On-Demand for the burst costs considerably more than Spot for a workload that tolerates interruption.
169:
AWS Shield Advanced provides enhanced protection against large and sophisticated DDoS attacks on resources like an Application Load Balancer, with always-on detection, automatic mitigations, 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team and cost protection against attack-driven scaling charges.

Why not the others: Amazon Inspector assesses workloads for vulnerabilities and cannot be attached to an ALB. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. GuardDuty detects threats but does not mitigate a DDoS attack.
171:
Traffic spikes only during the holiday season, so the platform must scale elastically and cost nothing when idle. Amazon API Gateway exposes the REST API and AWS Lambda performs the tax computation, scaling automatically per request with no capacity to plan.

Why not the others: a single EC2 instance is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Two fixed instances behind an ALB still need manual resizing for the seasonal peak. Fronting an EC2-hosted API with API Gateway (D) adds a layer but leaves the same non-elastic backend.
173:
The videos and images are identical for all users, so they are ideal for edge caching. An Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket serves the files from the location closest to each user and drastically reduces requests reaching the origin, which also lowers S3 request and transfer costs.

Why not the others: Global Accelerator optimizes network paths but does not cache static content. ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) is an in-memory data store for application data, deployed in one Region, and is not a media delivery mechanism for millions of worldwide users.
174:
Every instance sits in a single Availability Zone, so an AZ failure takes the whole tier down. Spreading the same six instances as three in each of two Availability Zones within the Auto Scaling group makes the tier highly available, and it requires no application changes since the ALB already balances across AZs.

Why not the others: an Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions, so A is not possible. A template for manual disaster recovery in another Region is not high availability. The ALB's routing algorithm has nothing to do with AZ resilience.
175:
The database is overwhelmed by open connections, which is what happens when Lambda scales out and each concurrent execution opens its own connection. Amazon RDS Proxy pools and shares those connections, keeping the count on the database low, and adopting it means only changing the endpoint the function connects to — the least possible application change.

Why not the others: provisioned concurrency does not reduce connection count, and a global database is for multi-Region reads. A read replica in another Region does not help write-heavy order processing and needs routing logic. Migrating to DynamoDB is a rewrite of the data layer.
176:
A VPC endpoint for DynamoDB (a gateway endpoint) lets instances in private subnets reach the table over the AWS private network. No internet gateway, no NAT, and the traffic never leaves AWS; an endpoint policy can further restrict which tables are reachable.

Why not the others: a NAT gateway or an internet gateway both route the traffic over the public internet. A NAT instance in a private subnet cannot provide internet access at all and is self-managed.
177:
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. It delivers microsecond reads, is fully managed, and is API-compatible with DynamoDB — so the application does not need to be reconfigured beyond pointing at the DAX endpoint, and there is no caching logic to write.

Why not the others: ElastiCache for Redis or Memcached requires the application to implement cache population and invalidation itself, which is both a reconfiguration and added operational work. Global tables replicate across Regions for availability, not to speed up reads in one Region.
180:
Two different threats need two different services. AWS WAF blocks web exploits such as SQL injection, and it integrates with Amazon API Gateway — which is the public entry point for the APIs. AWS Shield Advanced provides detection and mitigation of large, sophisticated DDoS attacks, and it can protect the Network Load Balancer (through its Elastic IP addresses).

Why not the others: AWS WAF cannot be attached to a Network Load Balancer, so A is not possible. Shield Standard is automatically on for everyone and does not cover sophisticated attacks, and GuardDuty only detects threats.
181:
The producers and consumers must be decoupled and each record processed once; order does not matter. An SQS standard queue does exactly that: producers write messages, consumers pull and process them independently, and the queue absorbs bursts and buffers work so services can scale separately.

Why not the others: SNS pushes the same message to every subscriber, which duplicates the work rather than distributing it. Using a Lambda function as a message relay is a hand-built queue without durability guarantees. DynamoDB Streams is a change feed for a table, an awkward and costlier substitute for a message queue.
182:
Amazon RDS for MySQL with Multi-AZ replicates every transaction synchronously to a standby in another Availability Zone, so each transaction is committed on at least two nodes and failover is automatic — minimizing both data loss and downtime after the outage the company suffered.

Why not the others: RDS Multi-AZ does not offer synchronous replication to three nodes in the way A describes. Cross-Region read replicas replicate asynchronously, so recent transactions can be lost. Self-managing MySQL on EC2 with a Lambda-based replication scheme is fragile and not synchronous.
183:
Minimal maintenance plus the fastest possible scaling of both reads and writes points to a fully serverless stack: S3 for static content, API Gateway with Lambda for the dynamic tier, DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode for a database that absorbs traffic changes instantly with no capacity planning, and CloudFront for global delivery.

Why not the others: Aurora Auto Scaling adds read replicas but cannot scale write capacity quickly, and provisioning replicas takes minutes. The EC2-based options (C and D) reintroduce servers to patch, and provisioned DynamoDB write capacity does not adapt as fast as on-demand.
185:
In ECS, the permissions an application inside a container needs are granted through the task role, specified as taskRoleArn in the task definition. The container then gets temporary credentials for that role automatically, with no keys to distribute.

Why not the others: there is no generic "S3 role" to edit. Security groups control network reachability, not API authorization. Creating an IAM user and launching instances "logged in as this account" is not how instance credentials work and would mean long-lived keys.
187:
Both tiers must be highly available with as little manual intervention as possible. An Amazon RDS DB instance in Multi-AZ mode replicates synchronously to a standby in another AZ and fails over automatically. An ECS cluster with the Fargate launch type runs the containers with no instances to manage and spreads tasks across AZs.

Why not the others: read replicas (B) improve read scaling but do not fail over automatically the way Multi-AZ does. A self-built Docker cluster on EC2 and the ECS EC2 launch type both leave the underlying instances for the company to manage.
217:
Up to 30 minutes of downtime and some data loss is tolerable, and the secondary does not need to serve load while the primary is healthy — that is a pilot light / warm standby pattern. Deploying the infrastructure in the second Region ahead of time, configuring Route 53 active-passive failover, and keeping an Aurora Replica in that Region gives fast promotion within the RTO at low cost.

Why not the others: active-active configurations (B and C) send live traffic to the second Region, which the requirements explicitly say is unnecessary and which costs more. Restoring from a snapshot (C) or building infrastructure from backups after the fact (D) will not reliably meet a 30-minute RTO.
218:
Two layers must both allow the traffic. The security group needs an inbound rule for TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (the default security group has no inbound rules for outside traffic). Network ACLs are stateless, so the ACL needs an inbound rule for TCP 443 and a separate outbound rule for the ephemeral port range 32768-65535, which is where the client's return traffic is addressed.

Why not the others: an outbound-only security group rule does not permit inbound requests. An ACL rule that only allows inbound 443 (C) blocks the responses. Option D allows 443 in both directions but not the ephemeral ports the replies actually use.
252:
The files must be reachable simultaneously from multiple EC2 instances, must grow over time and must be redundant. Amazon EFS is a shared, elastic NFS file system that many instances can mount at once and that stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones.

Why not the others: an EBS volume normally attaches to a single instance in a single AZ and has a fixed size. Glacier Deep Archive is an archive tier with retrieval delays, not live shared storage. AWS Backup is a backup orchestration service, not a file system.
259:
AWS Backup centralizes backups across services: create a backup vault, define a plan with a daily schedule and a 2-year expiration, and assign the RDS DB instances to it. RDS backups taken this way are consistent and restorable, and retention is enforced automatically.

Why not the others: automated RDS snapshot retention maxes out at 35 days, so B cannot hold 2 years, and DLM manages EBS snapshots, not RDS. Transaction logs in CloudWatch Logs are not restorable backups. A DMS CDC stream to S3 produces change files, not consistent restorable backups.
267:
Kinesis Data Firehose is the fully managed delivery stream: it ingests near real time, encrypts the data, converts records to Apache Parquet natively, and writes them to a central S3 location — no shards or cluster to manage. Kinesis Data Analytics then analyzes the stream, also without servers.

Why not the others: the options built on a Kinesis data stream (A and B) require managing shards and extra Lambda plumbing to reach S3. An EMR cluster (B and C) is infrastructure the company would have to run and tune.
270:
The requirement is that the data be encrypted before it is uploaded. Only client-side encryption does that: the application encrypts the object locally, then sends the already-encrypted bytes over HTTPS, which also satisfies encryption in transit.

Why not the others: all forms of server-side encryption (B, C and D) encrypt after the data arrives at S3, so the data is not encrypted at rest before upload as required.
272:
CloudFront can sit in front of an Application Load Balancer as its origin, so the existing single-Region architecture stays exactly as it is. Requests travel over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location, cutting latency worldwide, and adding Accept-Language to the cache key lets CloudFront cache a separate copy per language.

Why not the others: moving to an S3-hosted site (A) discards the dynamic application. API Gateway in front of an ALB adds a layer without edge presence. Running NGINX caches on EC2 in every Region is exactly the multi-Region rebuild the company wants to avoid.
275:
The slowdown happens at the start of the day, when the group is still at 2 instances and scaling is too slow to catch up. Making the target tracking policy more sensitive — a lower CPU threshold plus a shorter cooldown — makes the group start adding instances earlier and more frequently, without paying for 20 instances that may not be needed.

Why not the others: jumping straight to 20 instances (A and D) costs the most and wastes capacity, and setting the minimum to 20 also prevents scaling back down. Step scaling is a valid mechanism but target tracking maintains the desired utilization automatically and is the better fit here.
291:
CloudFront offers two mechanisms to restrict access to private content. Signed cookies work for users whose URLs are hardcoded and cannot be changed, since the authorization travels in the cookie rather than in the URL. Signed URLs work for the custom HTTP client that does not support cookies. Using both covers every group of users with the least disruption.

Why not the others: AppSync is a managed GraphQL service, JWT is not a CloudFront access-control mechanism for S3 origins, and Secrets Manager stores secrets rather than authorizing content requests.
293:
A Storage Gateway stored volume keeps the complete dataset on premises, so users retain immediate, low-latency access to all of it, while the gateway asynchronously and securely backs the data up to AWS as EBS snapshots. That matches "maintain local access to all the data while it is backed up on AWS".

Why not the others: a cached volume keeps only the frequently used subset locally, so access to the rest is not immediate. Snowball and Snowball Edge are one-time bulk transfer devices, not an ongoing automated backup solution.
317:
AWS Glue is the serverless ETL service: a scheduled job reads the .csv files from S3, converts them and loads the results into Amazon Redshift, which the COTS application can query. No servers, no cluster, no custom code to maintain.

Why not the others: a Python script on EC2 produces .sql files, which the COTS application cannot read either, and adds a server to run. DynamoDB is not one of the two sources the application supports. Launching an EMR cluster weekly is heavier infrastructure and does not meet a continuous need.
323:
The badge readers send HTTPS messages, so the entry point is an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint, which is highly available by default. It invokes a Lambda function to process each scan, and the results land in DynamoDB, where the security team can query and analyze them. Every component is managed and scales with the message rate.

Why not the others: a single EC2 instance is a single point of failure. Route 53 resolves DNS and cannot invoke Lambda functions as an endpoint. A Site-to-Site VPN with an S3 gateway endpoint requires network changes at the facility and gives the readers no HTTPS API to call.
324:
The existing server already mounts the volume over iSCSI, and a Storage Gateway Volume Gateway presents iSCSI volumes — so nothing on the application side changes. With hundreds of TB of data, a cached volume is the practical choice: the full dataset lives in AWS with a local cache for the working set, and scheduled snapshots provide the DR copy that can be restored to an EBS volume attached to an EC2 instance.

Why not the others: an S3 File Gateway would force applications to switch to NFS. A tape gateway is a backup target, not a live volume. A stored volume requires enough on-premises disk for the entire hundreds of TB dataset, which is far more infrastructure change.
329:
Amazon Inspector continually scans EC2 instances for software vulnerabilities, and AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager applies patches on a defined schedule and reports the compliance status of every instance. Together they cover scanning, patching and reporting across a large fleet.

Why not the others: Macie classifies sensitive data in S3. GuardDuty analyzes account and network activity for threats, and Session Manager provides shell access rather than patch orchestration. Detective investigates security findings; it does not scan for vulnerabilities.
338:
An Aurora global database replicates storage to the secondary Region with typical lag under a second and supports fast promotion for DR. A secondary Region requires at least one DB instance in the cluster, so the cost-effective design is a global database with a single, small instance in the secondary Region.
