Why not the others: B and C propose removing the DB instance from the secondary Region, which is not a supported configuration. Self-managed binary log replication adds operational work and higher lag than Aurora's storage-level replication.
343:
An Aurora global database gives cross-Region disaster recovery as a managed feature: the primary cluster runs in the main Region and a secondary cluster in the DR Region, replicated at the storage layer with sub-second lag and promotable in about a minute. Moving off the self-managed EC2 MySQL instance also removes backup and patching work.

Why not the others: replicating between EC2 instances keeps all the operational burden. RDS Multi-AZ with replicas in other AZs stays within one Region, so it does not satisfy the multi-Region requirement. Restoring backups from a replicated S3 bucket is a manual, slow recovery process.
353:
The workload needs about 1,000 IOPS with headroom for 2,000. A gp2 volume delivers 3 IOPS per GB, so a 1 TB gp2 volume provides 3,000 IOPS baseline — comfortably double the peak — at a fraction of the cost of Provisioned IOPS. Running it as a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL instance makes the tier fully managed, highly available and fault tolerant.

Why not the others: io2 Block Express is built for far higher IOPS and costs much more than this workload needs. S3 Intelligent-Tiering is object storage, not a database volume. Two EC2 instances in active-passive mode is neither fully managed nor automatic.
377:
EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause an instance in the Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait state, which is precisely the window needed to run a script that registers the instance with the auditing system at launch and reports at termination. Nothing else can reliably capture the termination event.

Why not the others: a scheduled Lambda function polls rather than reacting to launches and terminations. User data runs only at launch, never at termination. An Auto Scaling group does not invoke scripts on the operating system directly — that is exactly what lifecycle hooks are for.
385:
Least privilege means each tier accepts traffic only from the tier in front of it. The web servers' security group should allow port 443 from the load balancer's security group — not from the whole internet, since the ALB is the only client that reaches them — and the MySQL security group should allow port 3306 from the web servers' security group.

Why not the others: allowing 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on the web servers (A) is broader than needed. Network ACLs (B and D) operate on CIDR ranges and cannot reference security groups at all, so those options are not implementable.
392:
Customers are global and have dynamic IP addresses, so the web tier must accept HTTPS from anywhere: inbound port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. The database must never be reachable from the internet, so its security group allows inbound port 3306 only from the web servers' security group.

Why not the others: allowlisting customer IP addresses (B and C) is impossible when those addresses change constantly. Opening port 3306 to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the database to the internet.
419:
Two complementary controls. A service control policy attached to the root OU that denies ec2:CreateVolume when ec2:Encrypted is false is a guardrail that applies to every principal in every account, including root users. Turning on the default EBS volume encryption setting means volumes are encrypted automatically, so employees do not have to do anything differently — that is what keeps the effect on them minimal.

Why not the others: permission boundaries attach to IAM principals, not to an OU, and do not restrict the root user. Editing IAM policies account by account is error-prone and also misses the root user. Setting the account attribute in one account's console (A) is per-account and per-Region rather than organization-wide.
421:
AWS Transfer Family provides the serverless managed SFTP service. Backing it with Amazon EFS gives high IOPS POSIX file storage that resembles the shared storage the Linux servers used, and it supports POSIX user and group ownership so the company keeps control over user permissions. A VPC endpoint with internet-facing access lets the service keep elastic IP addresses while a security group restricts inbound traffic to the trusted IP ranges.

Why not the others: an EBS volume cannot be attached to a Transfer Family service. A public endpoint (A and C) cannot have a security group, so trusted-IP filtering is not configurable in the way required. A purely internal VPC endpoint (D) is unreachable from the internet users.
426:
The on-premises infrastructure is out of storage capacity and the data changes frequently, so AWS Storage Gateway is the right tool: it moves the data into Amazon S3 while keeping the on-premises systems working against a local gateway, continuously rather than as a one-time copy. AWS CloudTrail then provides the audit log the new regulation requires.

Why not the others: (Note that auditing access at all levels of the stored data normally means enabling CloudTrail data events, not just management events; the study key selects the Storage Gateway option.) DataSync, Snowcone and Transfer Acceleration are all one-time or bulk transfer mechanisms that do not solve the ongoing capacity problem.
443:
The users are spread worldwide and both upload and download multi-gigabyte objects. S3 Transfer Acceleration routes those transfers to the nearest CloudFront edge location and then over the optimized AWS backbone to the bucket, which speeds up long-distance uploads as well as downloads, with no infrastructure to run.

Why not the others: Cache-Control headers only affect caching of downloads. CloudFront in front of EC2 accelerates downloads but does nothing for large uploads and adds servers to manage. ElastiCache is an in-memory data store, irrelevant to large file transfer.
446:
The legal requirement covers new and existing data, so two things are needed: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year retention period, which nobody can shorten or override, and a way to apply that retention to the objects already in the bucket. S3 Batch Operations can set retention on millions of existing objects in a single job — far less work than recopying them.

Why not the others: versioning with lifecycle deletion and MFA delete does not prevent deletion for a fixed period. Governance mode can be overridden by privileged users. Recopying all existing objects (C) is a slow, expensive way to achieve what Batch Operations does directly.
449:
The application depends on third-party database features that need privileged access, which standard RDS does not grant, and the company lacks staff for backups and data center work, which rules out self-managing on EC2. Amazon RDS Custom for Oracle is the middle path: managed backups and infrastructure, plus the elevated database and OS access those features require.

Why not the others: RDS for Oracle blocks the privileged access and would force replacing the third-party features. Running Oracle on EC2 puts all administration back on the team. Rewriting the application for PostgreSQL is the opposite of a quick migration.
455:
Budgets are created from the Billing dashboard of each account, with the amount set per account so different accounts can have different budgets. To let a budget take action automatically, AWS Budgets needs an IAM role with the required permissions. Finally, configure an alert at the threshold plus a budget action that applies a service control policy, which is what actually blocks provisioning of further resources in an Organizations setup.

Why not the others: budgets are not defined under Cost and Usage Reports. Budget actions assume a role, not an IAM user. AWS Config rules evaluate and report compliance; they do not prevent resource creation the way an SCP does.
461:
The application uses both TCP and UDP and needs the lowest latency for a worldwide audience against a single-Region deployment. AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes users onto the AWS backbone from the nearest edge, and it supports UDP. Its endpoint must be a Network Load Balancer, the only load balancer that handles UDP.

Why not the others: an Application Load Balancer is HTTP/HTTPS only, so A cannot carry UDP. CloudFront is an HTTP cache and does not proxy TCP and UDP game traffic, ruling out C and D.
466:
The application is already stateless and the database is already Multi-AZ, so the only single point of failure is the single-AZ compute tier. Running the EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across multiple Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer removes it: the load balancer distributes traffic and the group replaces failed instances automatically.

Why not the others: cross-Region snapshots are a recovery mechanism, not high availability. Route 53 latency routing chooses between endpoints that must already exist in multiple locations. Option D adds DNS and a load balancer but never makes the compute tier span AZs or self-heal.
467:
Savings Plans and Reserved Instance discounts are shared across an organization when discount sharing is enabled, and that setting lives in the Billing Preferences of the management (payer) account. Turning it on lets the unused portion of the member account's Compute Savings Plan apply to eligible usage in other accounts.

Why not the others: the preference cannot be set from the member account. Moving workloads between accounts is a large change to solve a billing configuration issue. Savings Plans cannot be sold in the Reserved Instance Marketplace.
468:
The frontend must be a REST API, so create a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The backend containers run in private subnets, and the supported way for API Gateway to reach them privately is a VPC link (private integration) through a Network Load Balancer into the VPC.

Why not the others: a WebSocket API is for bidirectional messaging, not the REST interface required. API Gateway is not a resource inside your VPC, so you cannot simply attach a security group to it to reach private ECS tasks — that is why the VPC link exists.
475:
Amazon EFS is the shared file system that automatically provides a mount target in each Availability Zone in the Region, is highly durable, and is supported by AWS Backup, including copying backups to another Region on a schedule that easily meets an 8-hour RPO.

Why not the others: FSx for Windows File Server is SMB for Windows workloads and a Multi-AZ deployment exposes a single endpoint, not a mount target per AZ. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS do not provide a mount target in every AZ the way EFS does, and OpenZFS is single-AZ.
485:
Files are needed rarely, so the cheapest suitable class is S3 Glacier (Flexible Retrieval). The constraint is availability within five minutes, and Expedited retrievals return data in 1-5 minutes — the only Glacier retrieval tier that fits.

Why not the others: Standard retrievals from Glacier take 3-5 hours. Standard-IA and One Zone-IA give instant access but cost considerably more to store archives that are almost never read.
490:
DynamoDB has a native export to Amazon S3 that reads from continuous backups rather than from the table itself, so it consumes no read capacity units and does not affect application availability. It requires point-in-time recovery to be enabled and needs essentially no code.

Why not the others: an EMR cluster with Hive and a Lambda function scanning the table both consume RCUs and require code and infrastructure. DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda consumer means writing and operating the export logic yourself.
496:
The applications use two different storage types and must not be re-architected, so each is replaced with the matching AWS Storage Gateway mode: a file gateway presents NFS shares backed by S3, and a volume gateway presents iSCSI block volumes. Both keep a local cache on premises for high performance.

Why not the others: S3 cannot be mounted natively as a file system by the servers. Snowball Edge is a bulk data transfer device, not ongoing storage. EFS mounted over a VPN adds latency and does not cover the block storage requirement.
497:
The data output charges come from routing S3 traffic through the NAT gateway, which bills per GB processed. An S3 VPC gateway endpoint replaces that path: traffic from the private subnet goes directly to S3 over the AWS network, the endpoint itself is free, and in-Region transfer through it is not charged. Only a route table entry for the private subnet is needed.

Why not the others: a NAT instance still processes and forwards the traffic, adds an EC2 instance to run and is a bottleneck; putting one in a private subnet (B) cannot work at all. A second NAT gateway doubles the fixed cost while keeping the per-GB processing charges.
499:
At under 10% utilization the 1 Gbps port is oversized. Sub-1 Gbps capacity is only available as a hosted connection, which is ordered through an AWS Direct Connect Partner — you cannot create a 200 Mbps connection yourself in the console. A 200 Mbps hosted connection for the existing account keeps the same private, secure connectivity at a much lower cost.

Why not the others: ordering another 1 Gbps connection does not reduce cost. The console only offers dedicated connections of 1, 10 or 100 Gbps, so B is not possible. Sharing a connection with another account changes who pays, not the cost, and complicates security boundaries.
500:
AWS DataSync preserves Windows file metadata, including ACLs, and can write directly to an FSx for Windows File Server file system, so permissions survive the migration. If network bandwidth allows, deploy DataSync agents on premises and schedule the tasks. If it does not, an AWS Snowcone device can run DataSync agents locally, collect the data offline and then have the transfer completed into the same FSx file system.

Why not the others: every option that stages the files in Amazon S3 first (B, C and E) loses the Windows ACLs, because S3 objects do not carry NTFS permissions — so access rights would change.
503:
Cross-account access is granted by having each customer create an IAM role in their own account with the read-only EC2 and CloudWatch permissions and a trust policy naming the monitoring company's account. The company then assumes that role and receives short-lived credentials. The customer keeps control and can revoke access at any time, and no long-lived secrets ever change hands.

Why not the others: a token vending machine issues credentials for roles in your own account, not in the customer's. IAM users with access keys, however carefully stored, are long-lived credentials in someone else's account. Amazon Cognito authenticates application end users and is not a cross-account access mechanism.
508:
AWS Backup is the managed answer: one backup vault, one backup plan that selects EC2 instances by tag, a schedule of twice daily (well within a 24-hour RPO) and a copy action with us-west-2 as the destination — all configured once, with no scripts. The Data Lifecycle Manager AMI policy with a configured cross-Region copy achieves the same automated result for EC2 images.

Why not the others: any option that says "copy on demand" (A and E) leaves a manual step, so the recovery point cannot be guaranteed. Adding a Lambda function to copy backups (C) is custom code where AWS Backup already has a built-in copy action.
509:
The abusive traffic comes from a small number of known IP addresses, and it must be blocked at the web tier where it arrives. Security groups only support allow rules, so the immediate fix is an inbound deny rule in the network ACL of the public web tier subnets, which does support explicit denies by CIDR.

Why not the others: security groups cannot express deny rules at all (A and C). Blocking at the application tier subnets (D) is too late — the requests have already consumed web tier resources.
521:
Cross-account access should use IAM roles and temporary credentials, never long-lived keys. Each business account creates a role that grants read access to its DynamoDB table and trusts a specific role in the inventory account; the application runs as APP_ROLE and calls AssumeRole to obtain short-lived credentials for each table.

Why not the others: IAM users with access keys, even rotated manually, are long-lived credentials and the least secure option. Secrets Manager stores secrets but DynamoDB does not authenticate that way. ACM issues TLS certificates and cannot authenticate to DynamoDB.
534:
Logs are analyzed frequently for 30 days, so they start in S3 Standard; after 30 days they are only kept for backup, so transitioning to S3 Standard-IA lowers cost while keeping them retrievable; and an expiration action deletes everything at 90 days.

Why not the others: A transitions to the class the objects are already in and saves nothing. Moving to Glacier at 30 days (C) adds retrieval delay and minimum-duration charges for data that is deleted at day 90 anyway. One Zone-IA (D) sacrifices the high availability the requirements call for.
562:
A DynamoDB VPC endpoint is a gateway endpoint. Two steps are required: create the gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, and add the entry to the route table of the subnets so traffic to the DynamoDB prefix list is routed to it. From then on the API calls stay on the AWS network.

Why not the others: an interface endpoint for EC2 is unrelated. Gateway endpoints do not create elastic network interfaces and have no security group — those belong to interface endpoints.
571:
ACM cannot issue a certificate signed by an arbitrary third-party public CA, so the certificate must be created and signed externally and then imported into ACM. It is then attached to a custom domain name in Amazon API Gateway. HTTP APIs with a custom domain support a TLS 1.3 security policy, meeting the TLS requirement.

Why not the others: any option that says ACM creates a certificate signed by the third-party CA (B and D) describes something ACM cannot do. Lambda function URLs do not let you attach your own certificate.
586:
An AWS account can belong to only one organization at a time. The correct sequence is therefore to remove the R&D account from the existing organization first, and then invite it from the new management account to join the new organization.

Why not the others: an account cannot be in two organizations simultaneously. Creating a brand-new account and migrating every resource is far more work than moving the existing account. A management account cannot be a member of another organization.
629:
Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a fully synchronized staging environment running the new engine version. You upgrade and test the green environment while blue keeps serving production, then switch over in about a minute with no data loss. It is purpose-built for exactly this requirement and needs almost no manual work.

Why not the others: a snapshot plus an in-place upgrade means downtime and no opportunity to test before committing. Native backup and restore is slow and manual. Setting up a DMS replication task to a new instance is considerably more operational overhead than the built-in feature.
636:
The scalable, resilient pattern is to put a queue between the notification and the compute: subscribe an SQS queue to the SNS topic and use the queue as the Lambda event source. The queue buffers bursts of S3 events, retries failures and lets Lambda scale its polling independently, so no event is lost when the function throttles.

Why not the others: routing events through ECS or EKS before Lambda adds clusters to manage for no benefit. AWS Server Migration Service migrates servers and has nothing to do with event processing.
640:
Two grants must line up. On the function side, create an IAM role with the kms:Decrypt permission and use it as the Lambda execution role. On the key side, the KMS key policy must also allow that role to decrypt, because a KMS key policy is required for any access to the key. Both together let the function decrypt the objects.

Why not the others: a Lambda resource policy controls who may invoke the function, not what the function may do, so it is neither the place for kms:Decrypt nor a valid principal in a key policy. Attaching an IAM policy directly to a function (D) is not how Lambda permissions work — they attach to its execution role.
645:
An AWS KMS external key store (XKS) keeps the key material in an external key manager outside AWS, under the company's control, while KMS handles the integration with AWS services. It works with external key managers from multiple vendors, which is exactly the requirement, and it avoids operating any AWS-side HSM.

Why not the others: CloudHSM and custom key stores backed by CloudHSM keep the keys inside AWS and require you to operate the cluster. The default KMS key store keeps key material in AWS entirely.
655:
Two things are needed. The public endpoint must be an Application Load Balancer with the application's target group: it is the layer-7 balancer that supports session affinity (sticky sessions) through its target group settings, and it is the load balancer type AWS WAF can protect. Then create a web ACL in AWS WAF and associate it with that endpoint.

Why not the others: a Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and supports neither WAF association nor cookie-based stickiness. A Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting virtual appliances. Adding Elastic IP addresses to the instances bypasses the load balancer entirely, so there would be no endpoint to make sticky or to protect.
658:
Two choices minimize latency. A cluster placement group packs the compute optimized EC2 instances onto the same high-bisection-bandwidth segment of the network, giving the lowest inter-node latency for HPC. For storage, Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP is the file system that natively serves the same data over both NFS and SMB, which is the multi-protocol access the on-premises NAS provided.

Why not the others: a partition placement group deliberately spreads instances across separate racks for failure isolation, which increases latency. FSx for Lustre is a single-protocol parallel file system, and FSx for OpenZFS serves NFS only — neither offers NFS and SMB multi-protocol access.
666:
The application code cannot change, so high availability has to come from the architecture around it. Move MySQL to an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance, which replicates synchronously and fails over automatically to another Availability Zone. Then put the stateless Python application in an Auto Scaling group spread across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer, so a failed instance or a failed AZ no longer takes the site down.

Why not the others: a VPC has a single internet gateway and it is not zonal, so provisioning one per AZ is not a thing. Migrating to DynamoDB means rewriting the application's data access. DataSync copies files between storage systems; it is not database replication.
674:
The database is read-bound during traffic peaks, so the fix is to add read capacity and to stop re-running the same queries. Create a read replica and point the application's read traffic at it, which takes that load off the primary. Then add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster and cache the query results, so repeated reads are served from memory and never reach the database at all.

Why not the others: RDS has no auto scaling feature that adds compute to a DB instance. In a Multi-AZ deployment the standby serves no traffic, so it cannot absorb reads. Forcing the EC2 instances into the same Availability Zone as the database is a marginal latency tweak that sacrifices availability and does nothing about the read load.
679:
Three steps. Create the S3 bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled, which is what actually retains the backups and prevents them from being deleted or overwritten (enabling Object Lock also turns on versioning, so no separate versioning step is needed). Configure a default retention period of 30 days so every object the backup solution writes inherits it automatically. Finally, configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to expire the objects after 30 days, which is what deletes them once the retention period has elapsed.

Why not the others: creating a bucket with only versioning enabled adds nothing once Object Lock is on. A lifecycle policy cannot "protect" objects — retention does that. Tagging objects with a retention period is metadata with no enforcement behind it.
683:
Changes to the application must be minimal while resiliency improves, so each tier is rehosted rather than rewritten. Move the multi-node web tier to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, which replaces failed instances and spreads them across Availability Zones. Move the single-node MySQL database to an Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment, which adds a synchronously replicated standby and automatic failover. Neither step requires touching the application code.

Why not the others: putting a database in an Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer does not replicate data between nodes and is not a valid MySQL HA design. Rewriting the web tier as a Lambda function and migrating the data to DynamoDB are both substantial rewrites, which the requirement to minimize changes rules out.
